title: Your Voice Agent Doesn't Need a Frontier Model - Joel Allou & Ornella Bahidika, Microsoft

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is building realtime voice agent systems where latency (~950ms) is the governing constraint, matching the multimodal/realtime systems inclusion criteria for speech and streaming interaction. The demonstrated product is an AI voice tutor for personalized learning, while the architectural pattern is explicitly generalized to voice, realtime, and high-volume applications. The content spans architectural design decisions (model selection, state machine extraction) and build-time implementation of scaffolding around the model. The talk assumes familiarity with voice latency constraints, state machines, and LLM model tiers but avoids deep technical implementation details. This is a seven-minute conference presentation at AI Engineer with video demonstrations comparing model responses. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript with character-level evidence anchors of grade 'said_in_transcript'.

summary: Joel Allou and Ornella Bahidika present Ace, a live AI voice tutor that intentionally runs on a small model rather than a frontier model. The core argument is that voice agents live or die on latency, not intelligence. When a voice agent pauses for even a second, the user's brain perceives it as broken. Their latency budget is approximately 950 milliseconds to first token, which a frontier model that reasons for a full second has already exceeded. Rather than using a large model, they extract all thinking, reasoning, planning, and lesson-coordination logic into a deterministic state machine outside the model. The model receives a structured summary each turn and is left with only the task it excels at: speaking. They demonstrate this with two videos. The first shows Claude Opus 4.7 without scaffolding, where the model reasons through a question and takes a couple of seconds to respond. The second shows Haiku 4.5 with scaffolding, responding in about 900 milliseconds. The scaffolding includes a state machine that coordinates lesson steps, an intelligent layer that derives student mastery, and pre-computed logic for what happens next and how to answer. Joel is honest about the trade-off: small models without scaffolding tend to drift on long conversations and need strict rules. However, the scaffolding cost is paid once in code rather than on every turn. Their rule: pick the fastest model your latency budget allows, then spend the rest of your time building the scaffolding. This applies to voice applications, real-time applications where latency matters, and high-volume use cases. In all these cases, the model is the smallest part of the system.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction: Ace and the Latency Problem
sections.summary: Ornella introduces Ace, a live AI voice tutor running on a small model by design. She explains that silence on a voice call signals a broken system, and the real budget is milliseconds (~950ms), not IQ. A frontier model that thinks for a full second has already lost the room.

sections.title: Extracting Thinking into a State Machine
sections.summary: Joel explains that frontier models like Claude Opus 4.7 are good at reasoning but reasoning takes seconds. The team extracts all thinking into a state machine that coordinates lesson steps, derives student mastery, and handles what happens next. The model only receives structured output to speak.

sections.title: Demo: Opus 4.7 vs Haiku 4.5
sections.summary: Joel shows two videos. The first uses Opus 4.7 without scaffolding, where reasoning takes a couple of seconds. The second uses Haiku 4.5 with scaffolding, responding in about 900ms. The scaffolding makes small, cost-effective models viable for real-time voice.

sections.title: Trade-offs and the Rule
sections.summary: Joel acknowledges the cost: small models drift without scaffolding and need strict rules. But the cost is paid once in code. The rule: pick the fastest model your latency budget allows, then build scaffolding. This applies to voice, real-time, and high-volume applications.
